    #Question 6

    Let an​=(n+1)!(n+2)3n​.

    For n≥−1, the numerator and denominator are positive. Thus, an​>0 for n≥−1.

    (n+1)!(n+2)3n​=n+1n+2​⋅n!3n​

    (n+1)!(n+2)3n​=n+1n+2​⋅(13​⋅23​⋅33​⋅43​ ...... n3​)

    The subsequent terms after 33​ are all lesser than 1 since numerator<denominator.

    Removing those terms between 33​ and n3​, the resulting sequence is larger than an​.

    (n+1)!(n+2)3n​<n+1n+2​⋅(13​⋅23​⋅33​⋅n3​)

    (n+1)!(n+2)3n​<n+1n+2​⋅2n27​

    (n+1)!(n+2)3n​<2n2+2n27n+54​

    Using the Squeeze Theorem,

    0<an​<2n2+2n27n+54​

    Limit of lower bound: n→∞lim​ 0=0

    Limit of upper bound: n→∞lim​ 2n2+2n27n+54​=n→∞lim​ 2+n2​n27​+n254​​=0

    Thus, n→∞lim​ (n+1)!(n+2)3n​=0.

    #Question 7

    #Requirements for Integral Test

    Since n≥3, both the numerator and denominator are positive.

    Thus, the function is always positive.

    Denominator must be larger than 0 for the function to be defined.

    en−1>0 or en+2>0

    en>1 or en>−2

    n>0

    Thus, the function is continuous on the interval [3,∞).

    Let f(x)=(ex−1)(ex+2)ex​.

    (ex−1)(ex+2)ex​=ex−1A​+ex+2B​

    ex=A(ex+2)+B(ex−1)

    Substitute ex=1,

    1=A(1+2)

    A=31​

    Substitute ex=−2,

    −2=B(−2−1)

    B=32​

    (ex−1)(ex+2)ex​=3(ex−1)1​+3(ex+2)2​

    f′(x)=31​(−1)(ex−1)−2(ex)+32​(−1)(e2+2)−2(ex)

    f′(x)=−3(ex−1)2ex​−3(ex+2)22ex​

    Since ex>0, both the numerator and denominator are positive.

    Thus, f′(x)<0 and it is a decreasing function.

    ∴f(x) is a positive, continuous, decreasing function

    #Integral Test

    ∫3∞​ (ex−1)(ex+2)ex​ dx

    =∫3∞​ (u−1)(u+2)1​ du

    =31​∫3∞​ u−11​−u+21​ du

    =31​N→∞lim​ ∫3N​ u−11​−u+21​ du

    =31​N→∞lim​ [ln∣u−1∣−ln∣u+2∣]3N​

    =31​N→∞lim​ [lnex+2ex−1​]3N​

    =31​N→∞lim​ ln(eN+2eN−1​)−ln(e3+2e3−1​)

    =31​N→∞lim​ ln(1+eN2​1−eN1​​)−ln(e3+2e3−1​)

    =31​[−ln(e3+2e3−1​)]

    =−31​ln(e3+2e3−1​)

    Let u=ex.

    dxdu​=ex

    du=ex dx

    (u−1)(u+2)1​=u−1A​+u+2B​

    1=A(u+2)+B(u−1)

    Substitute u=1, A=31​

    Substitute u=−2, B=−31​

    (u−1)(u+2)1​=3(u−1)1​−3(u+2)1​

    (u−1)(u+2)1​=31​(u−11​−u+21​)

    Since the integral converges, the series also converges.

    #Question 1

    #Part (a) + Part (b)

    ∇w(2,0)=(4,9)

    ∂t∂w​=∂x∂w​⋅∂t∂x​+∂y∂w​⋅∂t∂y​

    #Question 5

    #Part (a)

    For n≥1, the first term of the sequence a1​=2022 whereby a1​≥0.

    Subsequent terms in the sequence can be found using an+1​=an​⋅(cos an​)2.

    Since n≥1, an​ would be a positive number, and square of cos an​ would also be positive. Thus, multiplication of positive numbers will give a positive result of an+1​.

    The lower bound of the sequence is thus 0.

    #Part (b)

    A sequence is monotonic if it is either increasing or decreasing.

    an​an+1​​=an​an​(cos an​)2​=(cos an​)2

    −1≤cos an​≤1

    Since ∣cos an​∣≤1, (cos an​)2≤1. Thus the sequence is decreasing.

    #Part (c)

    Since (cos an​)2≤1, an+1​≤an​⋅(cos an​)2.

    Thus, the upper bound of the sequence is 2022.

    #Part (d)

    Since the sequence is bounded and monotonic, by the Monotone Convergence Theorem, the sequence is convergent.

    #Part (c)

    an+1​=e4n+4+n+1(x+2)n+1​

    an​=e4n+n(x+2)n​

    n→∞lim​ ​an​an+1​​​=n→∞lim​ ​e4n+4+n+1(x+2)n+1​⋅(x+2)ne4n+n​​

    n→∞lim​ ​an​an+1​​​=n→∞lim​ ∣x+2∣⋅e4n+4+n+1e4n+n​

    n→∞lim​ ​an​an+1​​​=∣x+2∣ n→∞lim​ 4e4n+4+14e4n+1​ (L’Hopital’s Rule)

    n→∞lim​ ​an​an+1​​​=∣x+2∣ n→∞lim​ 16e4n+416e4n​

    n→∞lim​ ​an​an+1​​​=∣x+2∣ n→∞lim​ e41​

    n→∞lim​ ​an​an+1​​​=e41​∣x+2∣

    For the series to be convergent, e41​∣x+2∣<1.

    Thus, the radius of convergence is R=e4.

    −1<e41​(x+2)<1

    −e4<x+2<e4

    −e4−2<x<e4−2

    When x=−e4−2, the series becomes n=1∑∞​ (−1)ne4n+ne4n​.

    When x=e4−2, the series becomes n=1∑∞​ e4n+ne4n​.
